## Pulmonary embolism response teams

The PERT, modelled after the heart team and rapid response system concept, offers cross-specialty collaboration leveraging clinical expertise of multiple disciplines in the management of acute PE [[3](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C3), [12](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C12)]. As optimal therapies for select patients with intermediate- and high-risk PE are obscure with limited data, and as novel interventional therapies are rapidly evolving, implementation of the PERT may address knowledge and treatment gaps [[2](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C2)]. Assembling a group of several specialties is encouraged to enhance clinical decision-making in these areas of equipoise and to mobilise resources. By some reports, the PERT model may decrease time to anticoagulation, reduce mortality and improve quality outcomes and cost of care [[12](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C12), [13](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C13)]. However, criticisms of this model include limited robust data in support of benefit and a potential increase in the use of CBT following the institution of PERT at some hospitals [[2](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C2)].

The first PERT was formed at the Massachusetts General Hospital in 2012 and inspired a system implemented in over 150 centres internationally. The original model included cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, echocardiography, emergency medicine, haematology, pulmonary/critical care, vascular medicine and intervention [[14](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C14)]. Team structure is heterogenous across centres often involving 3–5 specialties with critical care, cardiology and emergency medicine commonly present [[15](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C15)]. Real-time convention obviates serial consultation and may facilitate multidisciplinary discussion and improve time to therapeutic anticoagulation, by contrast to a tiered approach [[5](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C5), [16](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C16)]. Beyond acute care, PERTs may facilitate patient follow-up and screening for long-term complications. In select cases of acute PE diagnosed at local hospitals, consultation with a PERT expert centre may offer guidance on initial management and facilitate transfer when appropriate [[17](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C17)].

The PERT Consortium was established in 2015 following an inaugural meeting of over 40 centres and now includes members from across the globe. This nonprofit organisation aims to standardise PE management, educate healthcare professionals and expand scientific literature; housing a large, quality database and partnering with industry on multicentre randomised trials [[12](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C12)]. The rapid adoption of the PERT model just over a decade since its inception has followed the evolution of advanced therapies. As standards of care for intermediate- and high-risk PE are in their infancy and rapidly developing, and as selection of advanced treatment modalities is highly nuanced, we believe the PERT is an invaluable resource in the management of patients with acute PE [[5](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C5)].

## Risk stratification

High-risk PE encompassing obstructive shock or cardiopulmonary arrest carries a mortality of approximately 21–42% in modern registries and requires an immediate therapeutic strategy, most commonly with the provision of thrombolytics [[1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C1), [18](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C18)]. Patients with intermediate-risk PE, or those with evidence of RV dysfunction without overt haemodynamic instability, represent a heterogenous population with short-term mortality ranging from 2–17% and a high potential for complications [[19](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C19)]. Within this category, intermediate-low-risk refers to patients with RV dilatation or dysfunction evidenced by either imaging or positive cardiac biomarkers, while intermediate-high-risk patients have evidence of RV dilatation or dysfunction by imaging and elevated cardiac biomarkers [[1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C1)]. Unless otherwise specified, intermediate-risk PE encompasses both categories in subsequent discussion. However, the risk of adverse outcomes varies not only between groups but within risk categories. Clinical risk models, such as the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index while sensitive, lack positive predictive value to identify which patients in the latter cohort may suffer from adverse short-term outcomes and potentially benefit from emergent reperfusion [[20](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C20)]. Accordingly, refining our approach to risk stratification is a central priority in PE care.

Guidelines include strict criteria with arterial pressure cutoffs and vasopressor requirements in defining high-risk PE; however, a large cohort of intermediate-risk patients display evidence of occult shock (evidence of low cardiac output/systemic hypoperfusion without hypotension) [[21](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C21), [22](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C22)]. In a study of normotensive patients undergoing catheter-based therapies, 40% had a cardiac index of ≤1.8 L·min·m−1 [[2](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C2), [23](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C23)]. Those with more severe derangements in their haemodynamic profiles may be at increased risk for early mortality and therefore benefit from reperfusion [[24](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C24)–[26](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C26)]. While this study is hypothesis-generating at present, the identification of patients with normotensive shock may allow for an individualised approach to risk stratification rather than broad categorisation and reliance on demographic variables.

The echocardiographic assessment of RV structure and function, while heavily relied upon, has important limitations. In a large meta-analysis of 63 studies, RV dysfunction carried only a relative risk of 1.5 for mortality among normotensive patients. The right ventricular to left ventricular (RV/LV) ratio and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), a marker of RV systolic function, were not significant predictors of death [[27](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C27)]. However, echocardiography provides valuable haemodynamic data. The left ventricular outflow tract velocity time integral, a stroke volume surrogate, is simple to obtain an carries an odds ratio of approximately 14 for adverse clinical outcomes among intermediate-high-risk patients [[24](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C24)]. Further, this variable is highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of normotensive shock in this risk category [[25](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C25)]. The ratio of TAPSE-to-pulmonary artery systolic pressure (TAPSE/PASP) is an echocardiographic marker of right ventricular–pulmonary arterial coupling, a comprehensive index describing the relationship between ventricular contractility and afterload. In a study of over 600 patients with intermediate-risk PE, TAPSE/PASP was a significant predictor of short-term mortality and outperformed the TAPSE and PASP in isolation [[28](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C28)]. Plausibly, incorporating a more advanced echocardiographic assessment of RV function will prove to be valuable in identifying occult shock and intermediate-risk patients at increased probability for adverse clinical outcomes [[6](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C6)].

Repeated clinical assessment tools incorporating time-varying components may have a role in the early identification of clinical deterioration and prompt institution of supportive and definitive therapies [[20](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C20), [29](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C29)]. The National Early Warning Score includes an assessment of vital signs, need for supplemental oxygen, and level of consciousness and demonstrates similar sensitivity and specificity when compared to the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index in its ability to predict intensive care unit admission and mortality [[30](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C30)]. Accordingly, this clinical risk model will be incorporated into an ongoing trial of CBT in acute PE [[29](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C29)]. The recently developed Composite Pulmonary Embolism Shock score includes RV dysfunction, elevated troponin and brain-natriuretic peptide, residual DVT, central PE and the presence of tachycardia; it is PE-specific, has been shown to predict occult shock among intermediate-risk patients, and is associated with adverse outcomes [[31](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C31)].

Laboratory markers such as serum lactate at a cutoff of 3.3 mmol·L−1 has been show to predict all-cause mortality in PE (OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.3–11.3) and may serve as a marker of hypoperfusion to aid in the identification of occult shock [[32](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C32)]. Along similar lines, a mean arterial pressure ≤81.5 mmHg has been shown to be a strong independent predictor of 48 h clinical deterioration (hazard ratio 3.25, 95% CI 1.89–5.21) in acute PE [[33](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C33)]. Rather than sole reliance of clinical risk scores focused on demographic variables and lacking positive predictive value, attention to time-varying components and markers of perfusion may refine risk prediction. How these indices are to be incorporated into practice in selecting ideal candidates for early reperfusion remains to be determined.

## Systemic thrombolysis

Several decades ago, J erjes-S anchez et al. [[34](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C34)] randomised eight patients with high-risk PE to streptokinase versus heparin; all patients treated with heparin died over several hours while those treated with streptokinase survived. While this study forms the basis behind the class I recommendation to administer fibrinolytics to patients with high-risk PE, numerous contraindications and concerns surrounding major bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage are important considerations [[1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C1)]. In a meta-analysis of over 2000 patients with PE, thrombolytic therapy was associated with lower all-cause mortality (number needed to treat of 59) at the expense of major bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage (number needed to harm of 18 and 78, respectively) [[35](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C35)]. In practice, thrombolytics are frequently withheld even when indicated [[36](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C36)]. Further, this reperfusion strategy may not be sufficiently rapid for select patients with catastrophic PE and alternative treatment modalities including the institution of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) may be an appropriate upfront strategy [[37](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C37), [38](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C38)]. However, VA-ECMO availability as well as rapid deployment may be limited by institutional capabilities and local expertise. Thrombolytic failure occurs in approximately 8% of high-risk patients and alternative means of reperfusion should subsequently be considered [[39](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C39)]. Even among patients with acute PE, thrombus may demonstrate elements of chronicity rendering it partially resistant to thrombolysis [[40](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C40), [41](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C41)].

Among intermediate-risk patients, thrombolysis is associated with a reduced incidence of the combined outcome of death and haemodynamic decompensation at the expense of major bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage [[42](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C42)]. Accordingly, this therapy is reserved for those experiencing haemodynamic deterioration despite anticoagulation [[1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C1)]. It remains unknown if the best strategy is a thrombolytic infusion or whether a bolus strategy is the best approach. Given the unfavourable risk-benefit profile of full-dose systemic thrombolytics (100 mg alteplase) in intermediate-risk PE, a reduced dose strategy (variably defined as 50 mg or 0.6 mg·kg−1 of alteplase) has been explored [[43](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C43)]. In a meta-analysis of three trials composed of 261 patients, reduced dose alteplase was associated with a lower incidence of major bleeding (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.12–0.91) with similar rates of all-cause mortality when compared to the standard dose [[44](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C44)]. When compared to heparin alone, reduced dose alteplase improved pulmonary perfusion and a reduced pulmonary artery pressures [[44](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C44)].

At present, the evidence base is insufficient to recommend a reduced-dose regimen with alteplase, or a bolus dosed strategy with tenecteplase, as opposed to an intermittent infusion over 2 h [[43](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C43)]. It remains unknown if alteplase or tenecteplase, a thrombolytic with greater fibrin specificity and longer half-life, is preferred [[45](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C45)]. The Pulmonary Embolism International Trial (PEITHO)-3 plans to enrol 650 intermediate-high-risk patients and randomise individuals to receive 0.6 mg·kg−1 (maximum 50 mg) of alteplase or systemic heparin. The primary endpoint will be a composite of death, haemodynamic decompensation or recurrent PE at 30 days with several secondary endpoints including severe bleeding [[43](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C43), [46](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C46)]. While catheter-based therapies have received considerable attention and are currently subject to several randomised controlled trials, these interventions may be inaccessible to many hospitals around the world. If the safety and efficacy endpoints of reduced-dose thrombolytics, as suggested by prior studies, are confirmed in PEITHO-3, we expect to see important guideline changes with respect to the management of patients in this risk category.

## Catheter-based therapies

Catheter-based therapies including thrombus fragmentation and aspiration were described in the early 1980s [[47](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C47)]. However, interventional modalities have proliferated in the past decade following the publication the ULTIMA (Ultrasound-Assisted, Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis for Acute Intermediate-Risk Pulmonary Embolism) trial, the first randomised controlled trial in the arena of CBT [[48](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C48)]. In the last several years, we have seen large multicentre registries examining CBT in intermediate- and high-risk PE with compelling results [[8](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C8), [49](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C49), [50](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C50)]. Large scale randomised trials are currently underway exploring several CBT modalities with respect to both short- and long-term clinical outcomes ([table 1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#TB1)) [[4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C4), [5](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C5), [51](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C51)–[56](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C56)].

Endovascular therapies fall into two general categories: 1) catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) in some instances equipped with features allowing for thrombus fragmentation, and 2) mechanical aspiration thrombectomy [[2](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C2), [57](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C57)]. Regardless of specific technique, CBT aims to rapidly recanalise the pulmonary vasculature, restore haemodynamics and improve RV function while minimising, or completely eliminating, the use of thrombolytics. Accordingly, patients experiencing clinical deterioration with relative or absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis may benefit from an endovascular treatment approach [[58](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C58)]. Whether CBT has the potential to mitigate long-term sequelae of PE is subject to ongoing trials [[4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C4)]. Presently, robust data supporting the use of CBT are limited and multidisciplinary clinical decision making accounting for patient factors and local expertise should be incorporated when considering such treatment options.

### Catheter-directed thrombolysis

Catheter-directed thrombolysis involves the percutaneous insertion of a 4–5 French infusion catheter maneuvered to the pulmonary artery with alteplase administered at a dose of approximately 0.5–1 mg·h−1 per side delivered over 12–24 h ([figure 2](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#F2)) [[57](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C57), [59](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C59)]. Beyond the reduced dose, direct infusion of thrombolytic to the thrombus is a cited benefit. At present, published randomised trials comparing CDT to anticoagulation alone are small and examine surrogate endpoints related to RV size and function [[4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C4)]. In the CANARY (Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis versus Anticoagulation in Patients with Acute Intermediate-High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism) trial, CDT was associated with fewer individuals experiencing the composite outcome of death or an RV/LV ratio of>0.9 at 3 months compared with anticoagulation alone (4.3% versus 7.3%, p=0.48) among 85 patients [[59](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C59)]. While this is the largest trial to date examining CDT versus anticoagulation, premature termination in the setting of the COVID-19 pandemic and underpowering were significant limitations to meaningful conclusions [[4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C4)].

Unlike a standard infusion catheter, the EKOS endovascular system (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA) is equipped with both a thrombolytic infusion lumen as well as one housing multiple ultrasound transducers thought to promote fibrin strand dissociation [[48](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C48)]. In a randomised trial of 59 patients, the use of the EKOS system was associated with a greater mean decrease in the RV/LV ratio at 24 h compared to anticoagulation alone (0.30±0.20 versus 0.03±0.16, p<0.001) [[48](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C48)]. At 90 days, RV dysfunction was more prevalent among those treated with sole anticoagulation. However, the clinical advantage of adding ultrasound transducers to the catheters has been brought into question. Among 81 patients randomised to treatment with either a standard infusion catheter or EKOS, similar reductions in thrombus burden were observed. Patients randomised to the standard infusion catheter experienced a greater reduction in RV/LV ratio at 48 h [[60](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C60)]. Underpowering and lack of standardisation with respect to thrombolytic dosing were important trial limitations [[4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C4)].

In a meta-analysis composed of 45 studies and nearly 85 000 patients, CDT was associated with lower mortality yet higher risk of bleeding when compared to anticoagulation alone (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.39–0.80 and OR 1.84, 95% CI: 1.10–3.08, respectively). However, when compared to CDT, systemic thrombolysis was associated with a higher rate of death (OR 2.05, 95% CI 1.46–2.89) [[61](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C61)]. In the absence of robust randomised data, therapeutic decisions must be individualised accounting for both risk of death and major bleeding. Several randomised trials are underway examining CDT compared to anticoagulation alone. The Higher-Risk Pulmonary Embolism Thrombolysis (HI-PEITHO) trial plans to randomise 406 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE with additional criteria suggestive of increased risk for early death or haemodynamic deterioration to treatment with the EKOS catheter or anticoagulation alone. The investigators aim to examine short-term adverse clinical events as well as functional and patient-reported outcomes over a 12-month period [[29](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C29)]. At present, CDT is reserved as one of several means of reperfusion for intermediate-risk patients experiencing haemodynamic decompensation or select high-risk patients with relative contraindications to systemic thrombolysis [[1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C1), [58](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C58)].

### Aspiration thrombectomy

Mechanical aspiration devices include the small-bore Indigo Aspiration System (Penumbra Inc, Alameda, CA) with a mechanical negative pressure pump, the large-bore FlowTriever device (Inari Medical, Irvine, CA) with manual syringe suction ([figure 3](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#F3)), and the AngioVac (Angiodynamics, Latham, NY), a venovenous bypass system with a suction catheter and interposed filter primarily reserved for the extraction of right atrial thrombi [[4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C4), [62](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C62)]. As aspiration thrombectomy obviates the need for thrombolytics, this modality may be appropriate for patients with intermediate- and high-risk PE with absolute contraindications to thrombolytic therapy [[58](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C58)]. Further, “acute” thrombus commonly displays elements of chronicity such as fibrin formation and organisation and is potentially less amenable to thrombolysis and therefore best treated with aspiration [[41](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C41)]. In a recent analysis of a large electronic health record database, aspiration thrombectomy was surprisingly associated with higher rates of major bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage when compared to CDT [[63](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C63)]. However, these findings are not consistent across the literature and demand further exploration [[64](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C64)].

In the single-arm EXTRACT-PE (Evaluating the Safety and Efficacy of the indigo aspiration system in Acute Pulmonary Embolism) trial, the Indigo Aspiration System was associated with a 27% mean post-procedure reduction in the RV/LV ratio among intermediate-risk patients, with only two individuals experiencing major adverse events [[50](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C50)]. These results were echoed in the recent interim analysis of the ongoing single-arm STRIKE-PE trial demonstrating a mean reduction in the RV/LV ratio by 26% at 48 h with only four of the 150 patients experiencing major adverse events [[65](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C65)]. The Indigo device is being subjected to a randomised trial examining several short- and long-term endpoints compared to anticoagulation alone [[4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C4), [52](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C52)].

The large-bore FlowTriever device was evaluated in the FLASH (FLowTriever All-Comer Registry for Patient Safety and Hemodynamics) registry composed primarily of intermediate-risk patients. In a report of the 799 enrolled individuals, aspiration thrombectomy was associated with on-table improvement in haemodynamics (19% mean increase in the cardiac index, 7.6 mmHg drop in mean pulmonary artery pressure) with approximately 75% of patients achieving minimal or no RV dysfunction at 48 h with only an 0.8% 30-day all-cause mortality [[8](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C8)]. Of the 63 high-risk patients in the registry treated with aspiration thrombectomy, several haemodynamic variables were shown to improve immediately with no reported deaths [[9](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C9)]. These results were echoed in the FLAME trial composed of 53 high-risk patients with only one individual experiencing in-hospital mortality. However, in the context arm (primarily patients treated with systemic thrombolysis), mortality was 29.5% and comparable to meta-analysis derived outcomes in this population [[9](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C9)].

The aforementioned results are compelling and, if confirmed in randomised trials, may alter the current therapeutic landscape. The PEERLESS II trial aims to enrol 1200 intermediate-risk patients in order to compare the FlowTriever system to anticoagulation alone. In addition to outcomes including 30-day mortality and deterioration, the study aims to examine several quality-of-life metrics at 1 and 3 month visits [[51](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C51), [66](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C66)]. Contemporaneously, PE-TRACT, a National Institutes of Health funded trial, plans to randomise 500 intermediate-risk patients to anticoagulation alone versus one of several CBT modalities with a focus on long-term outcomes including peak oxygen consumption at 3 months and functional class at 1 year [[5](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C5), [53](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C53)]. Over the coming years, we hope to better define specific indications for CBT, compare endovascular treatment modalities and understand their impact not only on short-term clinical outcomes but on long-term functional status. Pending these data, decisions surrounding interventional therapies should be subject to PERT discussion carefully weighing institutional and patient factors.

## Mechanical circulatory support

Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is a partial cardiopulmonary bypass circuit that functions to divert venous blood from the failing RV and return oxygenated blood to the arterial circulation. The RV is decompressed while systemic perfusion is maintained by the pump. The usual peripheral configuration includes a drainage cannula inserted into the femoral vein and a return cannula positioned in the femoral artery. Blood is withdrawn via centrifugal pump, progressed through an oxygenator providing for gas exchange, and returned to the arterial system at a flow rate of approximately 4–6 L·min−1 [[10](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C10), [67](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C67)].

With appropriate expertise, cannulation can be performed at the bedside outside of a procedural area within 10–15 min [[37](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C37), [68](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C68)]. Accordingly, VA-ECMO may be an appropriate support modality for the patient with refractory shock or cardiopulmonary arrest [[34](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C34), [69](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C69), [70](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C70)]. In such settings, thrombolysis may not be sufficiently rapid to offer haemodynamic stability [[70](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C70)]. Registry data suggest that among patients with PE suffering cardiopulmonary arrest, VA-ECMO may be associated with improved survival when compared to thrombolytics alone [[71](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C71)]. Importantly, antecedent thrombolytic administration is not an absolute contraindication to VA-ECMO. In a study of 83 patients with PE managed with VA-ECMO, 18 received thrombolytics prior to cannulation. While major haemorrhage was more common in this group, survival to discharge was excellent and similar to those managed with VA-ECMO alone [[72](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C72)]. However, the precise safe timing between thrombolysis and cannulation is unknown.

Once cannulated, patients may undergo surgical embolectomy, CBT, or be monitored on anticoagulation alone, providing time for thrombus autolysis. Guidelines suggest that VA-ECMO should be combined with a reperfusion strategy such as surgical or catheter-based embolectomy, yet data supporting this recommendation are scant [[1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C1)]. VA-ECMO combined with systemic anticoagulation as a standalone strategy has garnered attention and is supported by several reports [[73](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C73), [74](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C74)]. In a study of 41 patients with high-risk PE cannulated for VA-ECMO, 73% demonstrated RV recovery and were decannulated after a median of 6 days, obviating the need for additional reperfusion therapies [[75](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C75)]. Therefore, serial echocardiographic assessment of RV function to evaluate for recovery may be an appropriate approach.

In a meta-analysis of 39 studies and over 6400 patients, pooled mortality for high-risk PE treated with VA-ECMO was 43% [[76](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C76), [77](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C77)]. In the setting of out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary arrest from PE, outcomes are dismal, with only 16% of patients treated with thrombolytics surviving [[78](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C78)]. Indeed, conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation may be less effective with circulatory obstruction. In a report of the extracorporeal life support registry, patients with high-risk PE suffering cardiopulmonary arrest managed with VA-ECMO experienced a mortality rate of 68%. These statistics are comparable to the 71% mortality rate of cardiac arrest, regardless of aetiology, managed with VA-ECMO [[77](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C77)]. With appropriate expertise and careful patient selection, this approach may be considered in select circumstances of impending or active cardiopulmonary arrest related to acute PE.

Alternative right-sided mechanical circulatory support devices precluding the need for arterial cannulation are available. The ProtekDuo (LivaNova, London, UK) is a centrifugal pump with a dual-lumen cannula allowing for single internal jugular venous site access with inflow ports positioned in the right atrium and an outflow port situated in the pulmonary artery. Alternatively, the microaxial flow right ventricular assist device (Impella RP, Abiomed, Danvers, MA, USA) is inserted via the femoral vein and maneuvered under fluoroscopic guidance with the inflow port positioned in the inferior vena cava and outflow in the pulmonary artery [[10](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C10)]. While sole venous access is appealing, particularly following thrombolytic administration, diversion of blood to the pulmonary circulation may increase afterload to the already failing RV and hinder recovery [[38](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C38), [70](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C70)]. At present, literature informing on the use of alternative right-sided mechanical circulatory support devices is insufficient to make specific recommendations.

## Clot-in-transit

Free-floating right heart thrombi in the context of PE, referred to as clot-in-transit (CIT), have a prevalence of approximately 4% and are associated with a mortality of 22%; however, higher rates have been cited [[79](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C79)–[81](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C81)]. Despite CIT being considered a medical emergency, optimal treatment is undefined and prospective studies are absent [[1](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C1)]. Management approaches including anticoagulation alone, systemic thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy, and CBT can be considered. Given the rarity and critical nature of CIT, a PERT should be involved in selecting the optimal treatment modality. In a recent retrospective study of 35 patients subject to different management strategies, the use upfront advanced therapies (primarily CBT) was associated with a mortality rate of 8% compared to 50% among those treated with anticoagulation alone [[82](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C82)]. In a large recent meta-analysis including 492 patients with CIT, mortality varied by treatment modality with a rate of 12% with systemic thrombolysis, 20% with CBT, 31% with surgical embolectomy and 35% with anticoagulation alone [[80](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C80)]. However, given the retrospective nature of the studies, selection bias is an important limitation to the results.

The AngioVac (Angiodynamics, Latham, NY) system, a venovenous bypass circuit with a suction catheter and interposed filter is designed to remove CIT and intravascular material ([figure 4](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#F4)) [[2](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C2)]. The rigid cannula makes for thrombus extraction from the pulmonary artery a potential limitation, and a perfusionist as well as general anaesthesia are required. Alternatively, the use of the FlowTriever device has an indication for extraction of CIT [[83](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C83)]. Thrombus size, patient reserve, and relative as well as absolute contraindications to thrombolytics are among the considerations when selecting appropriate therapy. Those with large thrombi and limited reserve may be best managed with an interventional approach [[2](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C2)]. On occasion, CIT can become trapped across a patent foramen ovale (impending paradoxical embolism) extending from the right to left atrium and is associated with a high incidence of stroke. Surgical embolectomy is often recommended in such circumstances, however data informing management are limited [[58](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C58), [84](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/breathe/21/2/240100#C84)].

## Conclusions

Recent years have seen substantial evolution in the advanced therapeutic options available for acute PE. However, as the evidence base is not yet robust, specific strategy, patient selection, and local expertise are key components of therapeutic decision making. How best to determine which intermediate-risk patient will most likely suffer adverse short-term outcomes and potentially benefit from early reperfusion remains one of the central questions in the field. Whether the first-line approach to high-risk PE will change over the years remains to be seen. With several large-scale randomised controlled trials exploring endovascular therapies underway, we hope to see some of these questions addressed as the therapeutic landscape evolves. At present, the nuances and complexities are likely best addressed in a multidisciplinary approach with a PERT.

### Key points

*   Current approaches to risk-stratification are limited in their specificity to predict adverse short-term outcomes and a more nuanced approach including advanced echocardiographic RV assessment may have an important role.

*   Reduced-dose thrombolytics are currently subject to a large randomised controlled trial in intermediate-risk PE.

*   Several endovascular treatment approaches are available with a limited evidence base. Multiple ongoing randomised controlled trials in this domain may change the therapeutic landscape in acute PE.

*   Mechanical circulatory support may be an appropriate upfront strategy for patients with high-risk PE and refractory shock or impending/active cardiopulmonary arrest.

### Self-evaluation questions

1.   Which of the following has never been demonstrated with the implementation of the PERT model?

    1.   Decreased use of catheter-based therapies.

    2.   Faster time to therapeutic anticoagulation.

    3.   Improved quality outcomes.

    4.   Improved mortality.

2.   Which of the following is true concerning reduced-dose thrombolytics?

    1.   They are associated with similar bleeding risk compared to full dose thrombolytics.

    2.   In meta-analysis data, they are associated with reduced mortality in acute PE.

    3.   They are guideline-recommended as class IIa in the management of intermediate-risk PE.

    4.   They offer improved pulmonary perfusion compared to anticoagulation alone.

3.   Which of the following is true concerning catheter-based therapies?

    1.   Catheter-directed thrombolysis is preferred over systemic thrombolysis in patients with intermediate-risk PE experiencing haemodynamic deterioration.

    2.   Aspiration thrombectomy has been shown to be superior to catheter-directed thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE.

    3.   Catheter-based therapies may improve right ventricular function more rapidly than therapeutic anticoagulation.

    4.   Recent guidelines have upgraded aspiration thrombectomy to a class I indication in high-risk PE.

# Cover Story | Pulmonary Embolism: A Clinical Approach

Feb 01, 2025

##### Cardiology Magazine

![Pulmonary Embolism: A Clinical Approach](https://www.acc.org//-/media/Non-Clinical/Images/2025/02/CARDIOLOGY/Cover-Story-Main.png)

Pulmonary embolism (PE) continues to challenge clinicians with its complex presentation and potential for rapid deterioration. As the third leading cause of cardiovascular mortality in the U.S. –following only myocardial infarction and stroke – PE claims more than 40,000 lives annually and accounts for about 40% of the more than 1 million hospitalizations for venous thromboembolism in the country.1

Despite significant advances in prevention, diagnosis and treatment, this condition continues to present clinicians with complex decisions that demand rapid, precise judgment. Successful management requires a nuanced approach that begins with precise risk assessment and diagnostic accuracy, both areas in which cardiologists excel.

"Pulmonary embolism is a cardiovascular disease and we as cardiovascular specialists are ideally positioned to help manage these patients in the acute and even the chronic phase," notes **Geoffrey D. Barnes, MD, MSc, FACC**, in an interview with *Cardiology*. Barnes is a cardiologist and vascular medicine specialist at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.

"We are experts in cardiac biomarkers and echocardiographic imaging, which are used in diagnosis and risk stratification; we know how to prescribe and monitor anticoagulation; we have expertise in the cath lab and are the ones to manage critically ill patients with right ventricular (RV) dysfunction," he adds. "We also know how to manage patients on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and we know how to manage patients in the chronic setting who have dyspnea and often have limited functional capacity. We're really the specialty best prepared to manage most of the areas related to acute and chronic pulmonary embolism."

## **International Clinical Practice Guidelines**

Current guidelines for PE management include those issued by the American Society of Hematology (ASH, 2018), the American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST, 2021), and the European Society of Cardiology in collaboration with the European Respiratory Society (ESC/ERS, 2019).2-4 There is also a consensus practice statement from the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) from 2019 and a scientific statement from the American Heart Association from 2011.5,6

The most recent efforts, both released in 2023, include a clinical guideline on diagnosis and management of venous thromboembolic diseases and a "consultation document" on percutaneous thrombectomy for massive PE from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellent, the UK's public health body that provides national guidance and advice to improve health and social care.7,8

A review comparing these guidance documents highlighting areas of consistency, divergence and gaps was published in *JACC* last fall by **Marco Zuin, MD, MS**, **Gregory Piazza, MD, MS, FACC**, and colleagues (**Figure**).9

![Figure](https://www.acc.org//-/media/Non-Clinical/Images/2025/02/CARDIOLOGY/Cover-Story-Fig1.png)

## **Early Diagnosis and Risk Stratification: Cornerstones of PE Management**

"The first step in the diagnosis of PE is to use a validated tool to determine pretest probability. The degree of pretest probability will inform the decision of whether to order a D-dimer, which will either exclude the diagnosis of PE or prompt immediate imaging," says Piazza, a cardiologist at Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston, MA.

Early detection and diagnosis of PE starts with an initial patient assessment using validated tools (e.g., Wells Score, Geneva Score) to assess pretest probability, followed by D-dimer testing. In those with a low pretest probability, a negative D-dimer result excludes the diagnosis of PE, whereas a positive test or a high initial pretest probability requires imaging confirmation.

Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the primary diagnostic tool for acute PE across most guidelines. V/Q scanning is preferred in the ASH guideline in cases where CTPA is contraindicated or unavailable, and bedside echocardiography is suggested in hemodynamically unstable patients if CTPA is not feasible.

After a definitive diagnosis is made, validated risk stratification tools (mostly the pulmonary embolism severity index [PESI] or its simplified version [sPESI]) help categorize patients as low, intermediate or high risk.

"Once a diagnosis is made, the next important step is to consider the use of a Pulmonary Embolism Response Team, or PERT, to help guide early management decisions, facilitate access to advanced intervention, if that's necessary, and to make sure the patient has the right follow-up," says Piazza.

PERT teams bring together experts from multiple specialties, including pulmonary/critical care, cardiology, vascular medicine, interventional radiology, emergency medicine and cardiac surgery. They use a collaborative approach to quickly assess and develop treatment plans for PE patients, functioning similarly to other rapid response teams like stroke or STEMI teams, providing 24/7 availability for PE cases. The first PERT was established at Massachusetts General Hospital in 2012, and the concept has since spread widely, leading to the creation of the PERT Consortium in 2015.

For those identified as low-risk PE, PERT care is likely not needed. Risk stratification can help with, among other things, selecting the location of care (home, general medical wards, intermediate care unit or intensive care unit).

While effective PE management hinges on accurate risk assessment, which guides therapeutic decisions and predicts patient outcomes, these commonly used risk tools for acute PE have only modest estimating ability, notes Barnes. Also, as patients evolve clinically, risk profiles can change, necessitating reassessment and possibly an adjustment of therapeutic approach.10

In a recent validation study conducted by Barnes and colleagues of four commonly used risk stratification scores (ESC, PESI, sPESI and Bova), the researchers found only modest capabilities to predict seven-day and 30-day mortality.11

Says Barnes, "We have several risk stratification tools, and they are clinically and statistically significant, but they don't do a great job putting patients into buckets that clearly define who needs specific therapies. We haven't figured out how to combine all the different risk elements together to make a really clear schema that will guide clinicians."

At present, the ESC risk tool, which recommends using PESI or sPESI but also adds biomarker and radiological markers to the scheme, is probably the most advanced tool available, he says.

## **Treatment Strategies: A Tiered Approach**

Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of PE treatment for all risk levels. In fact, in patients with suspected PE, there is consensus to start empiric therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting diagnostic results if the pretest probability of PE is intermediate or high and bleeding risk is low.

***Low-Risk PE:*** About 60% of patients identified as having acute PE are considered low risk and do not require hospital admission.10 Those who are more symptomatic or have higher PESI scores may benefit from inpatient treatment initiation and observation.

For hemodynamically stable patients with no RV strain and normal cardiac biomarkers, anticoagulation becomes the primary focus. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have high-quality evidence supporting their use in low-risk PE and have transformed treatment protocols, offering clinicians a convenient and predictable management strategy that is noninferior in efficacy compared to vitamin K antagonists but associated with lower bleeding risk. There have been very few head-to-head comparisons of DOACs in this setting, so choice of agent can be guided by other factors, including pharmacologic properties, patient characteristics and patient preferences.12

***Intermediate-Risk Scenarios:*** About 30% of acute PE is classified as intermediate risk, with mortality ranging from 2% for those with only biomarker abnormalities to 10% for those with both RV dilation and biomarker abnormalities.10

For individuals classified as intermediate-*low* risk, those with RV dysfunction or biomarker elevation (but not both), standard anticoagulation is often first-time treatment. But for the 5% to 10% who have intermediate-*high*-risk PE, characterized by both RV dysfunction and biomarker elevation, progression to hemodynamic instability is a real possibility and treatment beyond anticoagulation should be considered, guided by the presence of myocardial strain or hypotension.

"The intermediate high-risk group is challenging because of our limited ability to predict progression and the current lack of clarity in terms of who might benefit from reperfusion therapy, whether that be catheter embolectomy, catheter thrombolysis, which uses a lower dose thrombolytic, or surgical embolectomy," says Piazza. Indeed, this is an active area of investigation (see sidebar).

***High-Risk PE:*** About 5% of patients present with high-risk PE.12 There is some heterogeneity in international guidelines with respect to the identification of high-risk PE although most suggest this subgroup should be defined as sustained hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP]  <90 mm Hg or a decrease in SBP ≥40 mm Hg from baseline or need for vasopressor support).

In terms of nomenclature, this category used to be referred to as high-risk of massive PE, but the term massive is no longer in favor. Some groups in Europe, notes Piazza, use the word "catastrophic" instead. "Massive implies a judgement on the anatomical size of the pulmonary embolism, which doesn't necessarily relate to outcomes. The term should not be used," says Piazza.

Aggressive intervention becomes imperative in high-risk scenarios and this treatment may encompass systemic thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy, and in select cases, even ECMO. These interventions demand rapid decision-making and a multidisciplinary approach to patient management.

Pharmacologic thrombolysis takes center stage in high-risk cases, with alteplase (tPA) considered the standard intervention, typically administered as a 100 mg infusion over two hours.

Clinicians should remain vigilant about absolute contraindications, including active internal bleeding, recent intracranial procedures, uncontrolled hypertension and recent hemorrhagic events. These considerations are paramount in preventing potentially catastrophic complications.

## **Advancing Our Practice**

"Pulmonary embolism demands a nuanced, patient-specific approach that challenges even the most experienced clinicians. Cardiovascular specialists are well-positioned to provide the individualized management, robust risk stratification, strategic anticoagulation selection, judicious use of thrombolytics and vigilant monitoring upon which success hinges," says Barnes.

"As the field continues to advance, with emerging catheter-based technologies, I hope we'll see cardiologists, both in the community and hospital-based, taking a more active role in managing these patients."

## **PERT Outcomes Data**

Despite advances in technology and the implementation of PERTs, standardized management practices and detailed outcomes data for these high-risk patients have been lacking. Kobayashi, et al., recently reported on the largest cohort of high-risk PE patients to date, using data from the PERT Consortium Registry, comprising 35 PERT centers in the U.S.1

A total of 5,790 patients with intermediate- or high-risk PE treated between October 2015 and April 2022 were included in the retrospective cohort study. Of them, 1,442 were classified as high-risk PE (defined as sustained SBP <90 mm Hg, need for vasopressors or cardiac arrest), including 197 catastrophic cases (high-risk patients in hemodynamic collapse). Outcomes were compared to those seen in a reference group of intermediate-risk PE patients.

Findings showed that advanced therapies, including systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed thrombolysis, catheter-based and surgical embolectomy, and ECMO, were used in 41.9% of high-risk patients and in 30.2% of intermediate-risk patients (p<0.001).  Compared to intermediate-risk patients, high-risk patients were more likely to receive mechanical circulatory support with ECMO (6.3% vs. 0.4%; p<0.001), surgical embolectomy (2.8% vs. 1.3%; p<0.001) and systemic thrombolysis (13.1% vs. 2.8%; p<0.001).

In-hospital mortality, the primary outcome, was seen in 3.7% of intermediate-risk PE patients, jumping to 20.6% for those deemed to have high-risk PE (p<0.001) and to 42.1% for those with catastrophic PE (p<0.05). Major bleeding rates were 3.5%, 10.5% and 23.3%, respectively (p<0.001 for all).

Predictors of mortality included vasopressor use (odds ratio [OR], 4.56; p<0.01), ECMO use (OR, 2.86; p=0.03), identified clot-in-transit (OR, 2.26; p=0.02), malignancy (OR, 1.70; p=0.01) and hypoxia (OR, 1.50; p=0.02).

Catastrophic PE patients had higher in-hospital mortality (42.1% vs. 17.2%; p<0.001) than those presenting with non-catastrophic high-risk PE. Catastrophic PE patients were also more likely to receive ECMO (13.3% vs. 4.8%; p<0.001) and systemic thrombolysis (25.0% vs. 11.3%; p<0.001) compared to non-catastrophic high-risk PE.

The authors conclude: "Disappointingly, our data continue to show significant mortality in patients experiencing high-risk PE despite technological advancements in catheter-based and surgical strategies as well as the larger national implementation of PERT teams." The extremely high mortality seen in the high-risk PE group with hemodynamic collapse (nearly six-fold that seen in the intermediate-risk cohort) is consistent with previous reports.

## **Emerging Frontiers: Catheter-Based Therapies**

The catheter-based therapy landscape for acute PE treatment continues to evolve dynamically. Concentrated primarily in specialized PERT centers, these innovative approaches offer tantalizing possibilities for targeted clot removal and reduced systemic thrombolytic exposure. Ongoing clinical trials promise to illuminate the full potential of these emerging technologies.

The study enrolled 550 intermediate-risk PE patients with RV dilatation and additional clinical risk factors.1 No significant differences in mortality, intracranial hemorrhage or major bleeding were observed between the two groups.

The primary outcome was a five-component hierarchical win ratio of all-cause mortality, intracranial hemorrhage, major bleeding, clinical deterioration/escalation to bailout therapy, and ICU admission and ICU length-of-stay during the index hospitalization and following the index procedure.

Researchers found this outcome occurred significantly less frequently with LBMT vs. CDT (win ratio, 5.01; p<0.001). With LBMT there were also significantly fewer episodes of clinical deterioration and/or bailout (1.8% vs. 5.4%; p=0.04) and less postprocedural ICU utilization (p<0.001).

The study enrolled 550 intermediate-risk PE patients with RV dilatation and additional clinical risk factors.1 No significant differences in mortality, intracranial hemorrhage or major bleeding were observed between the two groups.

"The PEERLESS study provides the first randomized data for mechanical thrombectomy and important new information to inform endovascular treatment selection for intermediate-risk PE patients in whom the decision to intervene has been made by the patient's care team," wrote principal investigator **Wissam A. Jaber, MD, FACC**, and colleagues.

Says Barnes, "PEERLESS taught us a lot about how to select between catheter-based embolectomy and CDT, but it did not teach us about selecting who needs an interventional therapy vs. who should just receive anticoagulation."

That question is being addressed in three ongoing trials: HI-PEITHO, PEERLESS 2 and PE-TRACT. "PE-TRACT, specifically, is an important trial because it is government funded and, essentially, device agnostic," says Barnes.

The PE-TRACT trial is evaluating how any device approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration compares to anticoagulation, and is "primarily looking at functional, patient-centered outcomes – peak oxygen consumption, walk distance, NYHA functional class, etc." Participants will receive mechanical thrombectomy or CDT; the exact technique and devices used is at the discretion of the endovascular physician, within parameters defined by the PE-TRACT Manual of Operations and accepted standard care.

![Table: Ongoing Trials in Intermediate High-Risk PE](https://www.acc.org//-/media/Non-Clinical/Images/2025/02/CARDIOLOGY/Cover-Story-Table1.png)

CBT, catheter-based therapy; CDT, catheter-directed thrombolysis; RV, right ventricle; PA, pulmonary artery.

While CDT promises reduced exposure to systemic thrombolytic therapies and potential for targeted clot removal, there are limited long-term outcome data. For now, CDT is primarily implemented in specialized PERT centers and is considered an emerging technology with promise rather than an established technology.

This article was authored by **Debra L. Beck, MSc**.
